title: The Winter Clock
premise: In the winter of 1916, Ansel Iversen keeps the lighthouse at Sker Point and the secrets of a coastal town that has survived by forgetting. When the army requisitions the harbor, its commander, Major Aldous Vane, seizes the town ledger of names, turning neighbors into suspects and old debts into evidence. Among those names is Marta Lindqvist, a lighthouse keeper's daughter who married a German naval officer, to whom Ansel once promised safe passage if she ever needed it. As storms batter the coast and Vane hunts a suspected signaler, Ansel must choose between the duty he swore to the light and the promise he swore to Marta—guiding her husband's ship past the mines while the town watches from darkened windows. The novel ends with Ansel extinguishing the great lamp for one deliberate minute, saving the ship but losing his post, his name entered last in the new ledger as both traitor and keeper.
about_author: Kestrel Crane is the pen name of a former maritime archivist who spent a decade cataloguing lighthouse logs from the North Atlantic coast. Their fiction has appeared in several small journals exploring memory, obligation, and the sea.

chapters.title: The Weight of Glass
chapters.summary: Ansel Iversen polishes the great lens and catalogs the silences he has learned in seven years of widowhood: the town's, his own, the sea's. A supply boat brings word that war has reached the shipping lanes. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: quiet dread beneath routine—the calm before requisition.

chapters.title: Ledger of Names
chapters.summary: The town clerk, Mrs. Okafor, records the winter census while gossip circles about Marta Lindqvist's letters from Germany. Ansel remembers the promise made on Marta's wedding day, seven years ago. POV: Ansel with a flashback. Emotional beat: nostalgia sharpening into guilt over an old vow.

chapters.title: Grey Uniforms at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Major Aldous Vane arrives with soldiers and a requisition order; the harbor, the boats, and the town ledger pass into military hands. Neighbors become informants overnight. POV: Mrs. Okafor. Emotional beat: humiliation and the first fracture in communal trust.

chapters.title: What the Light Owes
chapters.summary: Vane inspects the lighthouse and installs a signal watch, reminding Ansel the light now serves the navy. Ansel conceals his friendship with Marta's family. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: fear disguised as compliance; the keeper begins keeping two kinds of secrets.

chapters.title: Letters Under the Floor
chapters.summary: A package arrives for Ansel containing Marta's letters and a plea: her husband Karl's blockade-runner will attempt the coast in six weeks, and she asks Ansel to honor his promise. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the past demanding payment; love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: The Informant's Son
chapters.summary: Young Tomas Eriksen, hungry for army wages, reports a flickering light he saw offshore. Vane begins nightly interrogations. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: ambition curdling into complicity; the corruption of power seen from below.

chapters.title: Salt and Ashes
chapters.summary: A fishing boat strikes a mine; three men die, and the town buries them in frozen ground. Grief hardens into hunger for someone to blame. POV: Mrs. Okafor. Emotional beat: mourning weaponized—the town begins to want an enemy it can name.

chapters.title: Vane's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Vane calculates that catching a signaler will win him promotion out of this posting. He studies the ledger, circling names with German roots—including Lindqvist relatives still in town. POV: Vane. Emotional beat: chilling clarity of ambition; power revealing its appetite.

chapters.title: The Second Silence
chapters.summary: Ansel visits Marta's aunt, Greta, who knows about the letters and begs him to refuse the promise. He cannot explain why he won't. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: isolation deepening; loyalty becoming indistinguishable from betrayal.

chapters.title: Storm Signal
chapters.summary: The great storms begin; the light must burn through gales while soldiers occupy the gallery. Ansel learns the navy has laid new minefields unmarked on any chart he can access. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: dread recalibrated—the promise may now mean guiding a ship into death.

chapters.title: Tomas Sees Too Much
chapters.summary: Tomas catches Ansel burning Marta's earlier letters and hesitates over reporting him, remembering Ansel once pulled him from the tide. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: conscience flickering; the informant discovers silence has a price too.

chapters.title: The Requisitioned Heart
chapters.summary: Vane, unexpectedly human over shared whiskey, reveals his own losses and warns Ansel that mercy is a luxury the war has taxed beyond reach. POV: Vane. Emotional beat: uneasy intimacy between captor and captive; corruption shown as ordinary.

chapters.title: Greta's Testimony
chapters.summary: Pressed by Vane, Greta denies everything but gives up a name—not Marta's, but her own dead son's—to protect the living. POV: Greta. Emotional beat: sacrifice as strategy; memory wielded as shield.

chapters.title: Half a Promise
chapters.summary: Ansel signals a neutral fishing contact to warn Karl's ship of the new minefield, believing partial help honors the vow without treason. The message goes astray. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: the terrible arithmetic of compromise; good intentions scattering like wreckage.

chapters.title: The Night Watch Turns
chapters.summary: Tomas, cornered by Vane's suspicion, confesses the burned letters. Vane orders Ansel watched and prepares charges. POV: Tomas. Emotional beat: betrayal as self-preservation; guilt arriving too late to matter.

chapters.title: Marta at the Door
chapters.summary: Marta herself arrives secretly, having crossed under false papers to guide the ship personally; she carries the true chart of the minefield. Seeing her, Ansel understands the promise was never abstract. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: love made flesh and immediate; no more hiding behind distance.

chapters.title: The Longest Dark
chapters.summary: The storm peaks; Karl's ship is sighted. Vane, tipped off, marches soldiers to the lighthouse. Ansel must choose in minutes: obey the requisitioned light or keep the promise. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: rising tension to breaking point—duty and love finally face each other.

chapters.title: One Minute of Darkness
chapters.summary: Ansel extinguishes the great lamp for sixty seconds, using the blackout interval to flash the private warning pattern only a keeper would know. The ship turns from the mines. Soldiers burst in to find him standing in the dark. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: climax—sacrifice enacted, irreversible, serene.

chapters.title: The Last Entry
chapters.summary: Vane, furious yet shaken by what the darkness saved, enters Ansel's name in the new ledger as a traitor—but delays the arrest until the storm passes, unable to call murder justice. POV: Vane. Emotional beat: power confronting its own reflection; the corrupt man hesitating at the edge of himself.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers
chapters.summary: The town, having watched from darkened windows, says nothing when soldiers ask questions. Mrs. Okafor quietly alters the old census pages. Collective silence becomes protection instead of cowardice. POV: Mrs. Okafor. Emotional beat: redemption of the town's silence; memory choosing what to keep.

chapters.title: The Smaller Light
chapters.summary: Stripped of his post, Ansel tends the harbor beacon by hand, unpaid, while Marta waits out the war hidden in Greta's attic. They speak plainly for the first time in seven years. POV: Marta. Emotional beat: tenderness after ruin; love surviving without permission.

chapters.title: Spring Tide
chapters.summary: The war ends; Vane departs without arresting anyone, leaving the ledger open. Ansel lights the great lamp again, his name restored—or perhaps simply rewritten—and the novel closes on the first clean entry in years. POV: Ansel. Emotional beat: resolution—memory forgiven, duty redefined, the light kept.
